messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no bullet points.

Raúl Mendez had spent most of his adult life in courtrooms, speaking carefully, weighing facts, and expecting that if he did everything right the law would protect him. At 67, he was a seasoned prosecutor, recently semi-retired but still consulting on complex cases in a downtown office where the files were stacked neatly and the routines were predictable. That sense of order was shattered two years ago after an evening deposition with a defense witness ran late. Raúl accepted a drink from a man he had known professionally for years, and before he could fully register the strange heaviness moving through his body, he realized he was disoriented, unable to stand properly, and trapped in a hotel room where he was sexually assaulted. Even afterward, one of the most disturbing aspects for Raúl was not only the violation itself but the humiliating certainty that he had failed to stop it. As a man who had built his identity around control, competence, and protecting others, he was left with a grim, self-directed conclusion that he should have seen it coming, should have fought harder, should have kept himself safer.

In the weeks that followed, Raúl told almost no one. He showered repeatedly, scrubbed his skin until it was raw, and avoided looking at his own body in the mirror. He told himself that if he could return to work, keep his face steady, and stay busy, the experience would settle into the past. Instead, memories began returning in fragments he could not control. A cologne similar to the assailant’s would suddenly bring on a wave of nausea. The sound of a hotel ice machine in a corridor, the sight of a half-finished drink on a conference table, or the feel of a cramped elevator would pull him back into the room with terrifying vividness. At night he woke in a sweat, heart pounding, sometimes grasping for the sheets as if he were still pinned down. He would lie rigidly awake, replaying every detail and trying to find the one moment where he might have changed the outcome. Because the memories arrived so abruptly, he came to fear his own mind almost as much as the assault itself.

Raúl’s avoidance steadily narrowed his life. He stopped attending evening legal events and declined invitations to meet colleagues at restaurants or hotel bars. He insisted on daytime appointments only and began choosing seats that kept him near exits. In his downtown office, he would ask a staff member to open packages left on his desk because the sight of unfamiliar bottles or small sealed containers made him uneasy. He avoided all contact with the man who assaulted him, but the avoidance spread further than that; he no longer liked being alone with younger male assistants in enclosed spaces, and he found himself crossing the street if he saw someone who resembled the assailant in build or manner. He told himself these precautions were simply prudent, but privately he believed that if he let his guard down even briefly, he might become vulnerable again. This belief made the world feel dangerous in a constant, indistinct way, as though there were hidden traps in ordinary places.

The emotional changes were equally painful. After the death of his wife, Elena, five years earlier, Raúl had already been living with grief, but after the assault he became more distant and less able to feel comfort from family. He loved his adult daughter and grandchildren, yet he could not bear being touched unexpectedly, even by them. He was irritable over minor disruptions, especially at work when someone entered his office without knocking. He became ashamed of his reactions, particularly moments of involuntary arousal or bodily sensations that occurred in the aftermath, which he interpreted as evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with him. That belief deepened his isolation. He stopped going to Mass because the crowded pews and the need to remain still felt intolerable, and he began spending evenings alone in his apartment with the television on for background noise, not because he was interested in it but because silence allowed his thoughts to crowd in.

Over time, Raúl noticed he was constantly scanning for threats. In parking garages, he checked reflections in windows. At work he sat with his back to the wall. He startled easily at footsteps behind him and slept lightly, waking at the slightest noise from the hallway. His concentration deteriorated, and he found himself rereading the same page of a legal brief without taking in the words. The cumulative effect was a persistent sense that he was no longer the man he had been. He described feeling older than his age, “damaged,” and embarrassed that after a lifetime of prosecuting offenders he could not simply put this behind him. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent panic episode after a routine deposition in a hotel conference room, when the smell of stale carpet and disinfectant suddenly made him feel trapped and unable to breathe. He left the building shaking and ashamed, then realized that his world had become smaller and smaller around this event. He is now seeking help because he fears that if this continues he will lose the last parts of his independence and dignity, but he also hopes that with treatment he might sleep through the night, return to work without dread, and believe again that what happened to him does not define him.
